summary: The amud lists cress, purslane, eggs, and arugula; a digression notes that arugula brightens the eyes, and Rav Huna says one who finds it should eat it or pass it over the eyes. Rav Giddel said in the name of Rav that a guest should not eat eggs, because they lead to a seminal emission, nor sleep in the host's garment. Rav and Rav Naḥman, when traveling, would announce, "Who will be married to me for the day?" The concern that children of different wives might unknowingly marry relatives is answered by the Sages' publicity. A further concern is that a woman who accepts a proposal needs seven clean days; messengers announced the proposal before the sages arrived. Alternatively, women were designated only for seclusion, without consummation. The mishna then describes the High Priest's handoff to the priestly elders, his ascent to the House of Avtinas, the oath administered to him, and the Torah and biblical readings used to keep him occupied through the night.

display.title: Public announcements and the Gemara’s answers to objections about traveling marriages
display.whats: The five emission-causing foods are completed: garlic, cress, purslane, eggs, arugula. The arugula (gargir) digression notes it brightens eyes. Then a startling report: Rav and Rav Nachman, when traveling, would publicly announce 'who wants to be my wife for today?' and marry temporarily. The Gemara explains this controversial practice and its legal basis.
display.hint: How does the Gemara address concerns about Rav and Rav Naḥman seeking wives for a day while traveling?

learning.learnerQuestion: How could Rav and Rav Nachman publicly announce for a 'wife for the day' while traveling without this being a forbidden, casual sexual arrangement?
learning.coreTension: A report this blunt looks at first glance like scandalous behavior from leading Amoraim, so the sugya has to show what specific halakhic structure separates it from forbidden relations.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara raises two objections to the scholars’ announcements: the danger that unknown relatives might marry and the requirement of seven clean days. It answers with the scholars’ public recognition, advance notification, and an alternative of seclusion without consummation.
learning.resolution: The concern about unknown relatives is answered by the scholars’ public recognition. The seven-clean-days concern is answered by advance notification before arrival, or alternatively by designation for seclusion without consummation.

takeaway.text: The Gemara tests the traveling scholars’ practice against the risks of unknown relatives marrying and unnoticed menstrual bleeding, then gives a specific answer to each concern and an alternative account involving seclusion.

learning.ahaMoment: The Gemara gives two answers to the seven-clean-days objection: advance notice allowed the woman to wait seven days, or the scholars only designated women for seclusion without consummation.
learning.learningBlocker: Learners may treat the announcement as the whole account instead of tracking the Gemara’s objections and answers: scholarly identifiability, advance notification for seven clean days, and the alternative of seclusion without consummation.
learning.memoryAnchor: Five foods: garlic, cress, purslane, eggs, arugula. Traveling scholars: public recognition, advance notice and seven clean days, or seclusion without consummation.

argumentFlow.label: Five emission-causing foods completed
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The five foods are: garlic, cress (shachalayim), purslane (chalglogot), eggs, arugula (gargir). Arugula also brightens the eyes and can be rubbed on them. Rav Pappa says arugula is most effective when it grows on the border of the field.

argumentFlow.label: Rav Giddel said in the name of Rav: a guest should not eat eggs or sleep in his host's garment; Rav and Rav Nachman announce for daily wives
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Giddel (citing Rav)
argumentFlow.text: When Rav traveled to Darshish, he would publicly announce: 'Who will be married to me for the day?' Similarly, Rav Nachman made this announcement when traveling to Shekhantziv.

argumentFlow.label: Concern about unwitting forbidden unions
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov objects that marrying in different places could lead children who are unaware of their relationship to marry each other. The Gemara answers that the Sages generate publicity, so their children’s identities would be known.

argumentFlow.label: What about children from such unions?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: A concern is raised that children from the different marriages might be unaware of their relationship and could marry each other, leading to forbidden unions. The Gemara responds that the Sages are well known, so their children are identified.

argumentFlow.label: A woman who accepts a marriage proposal needs seven clean days
argumentFlow.speaker: Rava
argumentFlow.text: Rava ruled that any woman who is proposed marriage and agrees must wait seven clean days before marrying, because anticipatory desire may have caused her to not notice menstrual bleeding.

sourceRefs.note: Required wait of seven clean days after a woman agrees to a marriage proposal, in case anticipatory desire caused her not to notice menstrual bleeding

visualizableElements.item: A messenger announces the scholar’s proposal before his arrival - a woman agrees - she waits seven clean days - the scholar arrives and marries her

quizSeeds.question: Why was there no concern that the children of Rav and Rav Nachman’s marriages might unknowingly marry their relatives?
quizSeeds.answer: The Sages were well known and generated publicity, so the identity of their children would also be known, removing the concern that relatives might unknowingly marry.

quizSeeds.question: Why does a woman who agrees to marry the traveling scholar need to wait seven clean days before marrying him?
quizSeeds.answer: Anticipatory desire might cause bleeding that she does not notice. Therefore, once she agrees to the proposal, she counts seven clean days before marrying the arriving scholar.

sugyot.finalRuling: Five emission-causing foods are listed. Rav and Rav Naḥman announced that they sought a wife for the day; the Gemara answers concerns about unknown relatives and seven clean days, then offers an alternative of seclusion without consummation.

alternateAngles.desc: The Gemara answers that the Sages were well known. It further explains that messengers informed the women before the Sages arrived, or alternatively that women were designated only for seclusion without consummation, since an unmarried man's desire is more acute than that of one who has ready access to a wife, just as one who lacks bread in his basket feels hunger more acutely than one who has it.

glossary.en: A wife for the day of the scholar’s visit.
Seven clean days - observed after a woman agrees to a marriage proposal because anticipatory desire may have caused unnoticed menstrual bleeding.

prerequisiteKnowledge: The concerns of unknown family relationships and seven clean days after agreement to a marriage proposal

display.title: Teaching and reading: the High Priest’s all-night vigil
display.whats: The elders of the court pass the KG to the elders of the priesthood, who take him to the House of Avtinas and administer an oath that he will not alter their instructions. Throughout the night he is kept occupied: if he is a scholar, he teaches Torah; otherwise scholars teach before him. If accustomed to reading Scripture, he reads; otherwise they read Job, Ezra, and Chronicles before him. Zekharya ben Kevutal says he often read Daniel before him.
display.hint: How did they keep the High Priest occupied through the night so that he would not fall asleep?

learning.learnerQuestion: How does the mishna keep the KG occupied throughout the night when his ability to teach or read varies?
learning.coreTension: The KG must be kept occupied throughout the night, but his abilities differ: he may teach or be taught, and he may read Scripture or have it read before him.
learning.coreMove: The mishna offers teaching and reading according to the KG’s abilities: he teaches if he is a scholar, otherwise scholars teach before him; he reads if accustomed to it, otherwise others read before him.
learning.resolution: The vigil is adapted to the High Priest: if he is a scholar, he teaches Torah; otherwise scholars teach before him. If he is accustomed to read Scripture, he reads; otherwise others read before him.

takeaway.text: A person can be kept engaged through activities suited to his abilities: teaching if he is a scholar, or listening and reading when appropriate.

learning.ahaMoment: The vigil adapts to the KG: a scholar teaches, while others are taught; a practiced reader reads, while others are read to, keeping him occupied throughout the night.
learning.learningBlocker: Learners may miss how the mishna tailors the vigil to the KG: he either teaches or is taught, and either reads Scripture or is read to.
learning.memoryAnchor: Beit Avtinas: the High Priest is sworn not to change the instructed service, and the elders depart in tears. At night, teaching or biblical reading is used to keep him awake.

argumentFlow.label: High Priest handed to the priestly elders and taken up to Beit Avtinas
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishna
argumentFlow.text: The elders hand the KG to the priestly elders, who escort him to the Beit Avtinas chamber. They adjure him there, saying: "My Master, High Priest, we are agents of the court, and you are our agent and the agent of the court." They adjure him (make him swear) in the name of Him who housed His name in this House that he will not deviate from their instructions regarding the incense service or any other service he performs alone. Then he parts from them weeping, and they part from him weeping.

sourceRefs.note: Handoff to Beit Avtinas and oath

argumentFlow.label: KG is kept awake all night
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishna
argumentFlow.text: They keep the KG occupied throughout the night. If he is a Torah scholar, he teaches Torah; if not, Torah scholars teach before him. If he is accustomed to reading Scripture, he reads; otherwise, they read before him from Job, Ezra, and Chronicles. Zekharya ben Kevutal says he often read before him from Daniel.

visualizableElements.item: At the House of Avtinas, the priestly elders administer an oath and depart. At night, the High Priest teaches Torah or is taught; he reads Scripture or others read Job, Ezra, and Chronicles before him.

quizSeeds.question: Why was the High Priest kept occupied all night to prevent him from sleeping?
quizSeeds.answer: To prevent the High Priest from sleeping during the night.

quizSeeds.question: How were teaching and biblical reading adapted to the High Priest’s abilities?
quizSeeds.answer: If he was a scholar, he taught Torah; if not, scholars taught before him. If accustomed to read Scripture, he read; otherwise others read before him.

sugyot.finalRuling: They keep the KG occupied throughout the night: he teaches Torah or scholars teach before him, and he reads Scripture or others read before him.

glossary.en: The place to which the elders of the priesthood took the High Priest before administering the oath.

prerequisiteKnowledge: The High Priest’s oath at the House of Avtinas
Teaching Torah and reading Scripture as ways to prevent sleep

glossary.en: Seven clean days - required after a woman accepts a marriage proposal because anticipatory desire may cause unnoticed bleeding.
The House of Avtinas, to which the priestly elders took the High Priest and where they administered him an oath.

rashiTranslations.en: 'The cress' - karshin. 'Purslane' - polpor. 'The arugula' - aruga. 'Matzranaha' -
growing on the border, around which there is no other seed, so that it not weaken its strength. 'He shall not eat
eggs' - since they bring one to seminal emission, and it becomes shameful before the household. 'He shall not sleep in the cloak
of the host' - which he covers himself with by day, so that a seminal emission not be found on it. 'When
he happened to come to Darshish' - there he was accustomed to go
'Who will be my wife for the day' - there is a woman who would marry
me for the day, for as long as I remain here, and afterward she would leave
from here. 'This one alongside that one' - a son that he would father
in this province, with a daughter he would father in
another province. 'The Rabbis, they have a reputation' - and their name
is called after their children. 'She must wait seven
clean days' - from the day she agreed, lest due to
desire she saw blood. 'Mere seclusion' -
and they are not intimate with them, except that one who is married
does not desire like one who has no wife
Mishna: 'The elders of the court handed him over' -
to those who had read before him the order of the day. 'To the elders of
the priesthood' - to teach him the scooping of the incense
incumbent upon him on Yom Kippur, as it is stated
(Leviticus 16), 'and his hands full of finely ground incense'
etc., and it is a difficult service, as explained further on
(47b). 'The house of Avtinas' - they would make
the incense, pounding it and blending
its spices. 'And they administered an oath to him' - to ensure he was not a Sadducee
who would prepare it outside and bring it in, as we say
in the Gemara (below, 19b). 'My lord' - my master
'He withdraws and weeps' - explained in the Gemara (ibid.)
'If he was a Sage, he expounds' - on a matter of law, throughout
the night of Yom Kippur, so that he not sleep and have a seminal emission. 'And if
not' - he is wise and knows how to understand and hear a matter of
law, but does not know how to expound, they expound before him
'From Job and Ezra, etc.' - since these are matters that draw
the heart to hear them, and sleep does not seize him
